title: "Cameras On… Please?" Ideas for Turning Empty Squares into Faces
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Prompted by an Edutopia piece from Liz Byron Loya, Dave Stuart Jr. works through fifteen strategies for encouraging students to turn their cameras on during synchronous remote classes, explicitly trying, rejecting, or modifying each one based on his own teaching philosophy. He's careful to frame the goal not as compliance or surveillance but as relational; he wants to see and know his students, not control them, and repeatedly warns against language of coercion, arguing that behaviors can be forced but motivation can't. A student survey he ran mid-article surfaces an unexpected finding: the top reason students cited for keeping cameras off was self-consciousness about their appearance, not privacy, which reshapes which interventions actually make sense. Practical tactics he adopts include admitting students into the Zoom waiting room one at a time, so early camera-on arrivals create visible social proof for others, and Zoom's built-in 'Ask to Start Video' feature, while he explicitly declines gimmicks like mandatory icebreaker games or rubric-based camera requirements as too heavy-handed. The piece closes with Stuart's broader teaching philosophy that teachers need clearer thinking more than more strategies, treating this list as raw material for small, individually-run experiments rather than a prescription.
points: Stuart works through Liz Byron Loya's 15-strategy Edutopia list one by one, publicly accepting some (surveying students, Zoom's 'Ask to Start Video' feature, admitting students individually into the waiting room) and rejecting others (icebreaker games, rubric-based camera requirements) based on fit with his teaching style.

His survey of his own students found the single most common reason for cameras-off was self-consciousness about appearance, not privacy or bandwidth concerns as often assumed, which reframes the intervention as an empathy problem, not a compliance problem.
Stuart insists the ask must be framed in the 'language of community, not compliance,' arguing that coercing the behavior undermines the actual goal of building visible, known relationships.

The 'admit students individually' tactic is highlighted as unusually effective because early arrivals with cameras on create visible social proof for later arrivals, a specific psychological lever, not just a logistical routine.
quotes: This isn't going to be me wading into the Great Camera Debate of 2020 but is instead me processing strategies for getting more students to turn their cameras on during whole-class, synchronous instruction.
It's not about me stealing student autonomy or micromanaging student bodies or depriving children of privacy. But I do desire to teach and know my students, and seeing them helps me in that work.
As soon as you start using the language of compliance or consequences, you're trading behavior for motivation. Behaviors can be coerced, but motivation can't.

The most remarkable thing that I found in my survey is that the most common reason cited by my students for not wanting their cameras on is that they don't like how they look. That one made me quiet for a few days.

As students arrive, admit and greet them individually, and check in with them about camera use. You might be able to check in with only a few students before needing to 'admit all,' but those who arrive early and have their cameras on will gain comfort from being in a small group to start.
Normally, I say that we teachers need more techniques and strategies like we need lobotomies: not much. Instead, we need clearer thinking and a deeper understanding of the work that matters the most.

In this case, I've got a novel problem called the Great Ghost Plague of Zoomland, and so I'm looking for efficient means through which I can gain insight into the problem and run small experiments on solving it.
